lesson.title: Inheritance: Reusing a Class's Blueprint
lesson.summary: Inheritance lets a new class automatically take on the attributes and methods of an existing class, so closely related classes can share code instead of each one rewriting it from scratch.
lesson.body:
You have written classes before as blueprints for objects, using object-oriented programming to bundle data and behavior together. Inheritance is the mechanism that lets one class be built directly on top of another one. Instead of writing a brand new class from nothing, you can say "this new class is basically that other class, plus a few extra things," and Python will hand the new class all of the parent's methods and attributes automatically.

The syntax is simple: you put the existing class's name in parentheses after the new class's name. Here, Bird inherits everything Animal defines, without Bird having to rewrite a single line of it.

```python
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def eat(self):
        return f"{self.name} is eating."

class Bird(Animal):
    def fly(self):
        return f"{self.name} flaps its wings and flies."

b = Bird("Robin")
print(b.eat())
print(b.fly())
print(isinstance(b, Animal))
```

This prints `Robin is eating.`, then `Robin flaps its wings and flies.`, then `True`. Look closely at what happened: Bird never defined `__init__` or `eat`, yet `b.eat()` still works. When Python looks for a method on `b` and does not find it directly on the Bird class, it automatically checks Bird's parent class, Animal, and finds `eat` there. The `isinstance(b, Animal)` check confirms that a Bird object really does count as an Animal too, something the next section explores in more depth.

Why does this matter? Without inheritance, every related class would need its own copy of shared logic, and fixing a bug in that logic would mean hunting down and fixing every copy. With inheritance, you write `eat` once, on Animal, and every current and future animal subclass gets the fix for free. This is the core payoff of inheritance: less duplicated code, and one clear place to maintain shared behavior. The next several sections will unpack the vocabulary around this relationship (parent class, child class), the tools for controlling it precisely (`super()`), and the powerful things it enables once many classes share a common ancestor (polymorphism).
